title: Lesson 20: Simple Repeatable Workflows You Can Run Weekly
description: Turning saved prompts into a fixed weekly routine: the same steps, in the same order, on the same day, with clean handoffs and a check you actually run.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Simple Repeatable Workflows You Can Run Weekly", what distinguishes a workflow from a prompt?
options: A prompt is one request, while a workflow is a fixed sequence of steps run in order toward a recurring result
A workflow requires software, while a prompt does not
A prompt produces better output than a workflow
A workflow has no output that needs checking
questions.explanation: The lesson draws the line plainly: a prompt is a single request, while a workflow is several requests arranged so each step hands its output to the next.

questions.question: What does the lesson say about the check step in a workflow?
options: It can be skipped once the workflow has proven stable
It is the step you never skip, because it is what keeps a fast routine safe, and it is where you decide
It is only needed for financial or legal workflows
It replaces the handoff between steps
questions.explanation: The lesson ties the check to the series-wide split that the tool drafts and you decide, and calls the check the place where that decision happens for a workflow.

questions.question: Why does the lesson insist on a timebox for a weekly workflow?
options: It makes the tool's output more accurate
It stops the tool from running for too long
Because a workflow you can finish in a set window actually runs every week, while one that balloons into an afternoon gets skipped
Because subscriptions are billed in time blocks
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the timebox as a fixed amount of time given to the workflow, like forty-five minutes on a Friday, and says the set window is what keeps it running.
